schools.summary: Gill takes the 'fulness' for the whole terraqueous globe — land, water, air, and every creature, all the riches of the Lord; Calvin, while granting the riches are comprehended (as Paul proves), holds the Psalmist means chiefly men themselves, the earth's most illustrious ornament.

Henry presses ownership into stewardship — God let the earth to men as tenants, reserving the property, so a child of God never goes off his Father's ground; Spurgeon turns the verse against Jewish exclusiveness, the whole round world claimed for Jehovah, Christ ending the exclusiveness of nationalities.
Clarke hears the Sovereign Ruler, Creator and Governor of the soil though men parcel out its kingdoms, and sets the psalm at the bringing of the ark from Obed-edom's house to Mount Zion.

Keil and Delitzsch note Paul founds on the verse (1 Cor. 10:26) the liberty to eat what is sold in the shambles, and record the Talmudic duty of prayer before meat; Ellicott makes Jehovah's universal majesty the ground for demanding rectitude in worshippers.

Augustine reads the psalm of the Lord glorified early on the first day of the week, the world's compass become his Church, founded above the seas that their waves be subdued and above the rivers that worldly lusts be overcome.

debates.question: What does 'the fulness thereof' chiefly denote?

sides.position: all the riches and creatures of the earth — land, water, air, beasts, metals
chiefly men themselves, the most illustrious ornament and glory of the earth (though the riches are comprehended too)

outliers.note: Reads the whole verse allegorically and typologically — of the risen Lord glorified on the first day of the week, the compass of the world become his Church founded above the seas and rivers of worldly lust.

schools.summary: Gill weighs the preposition ('upon'/'with'/'by' the seas), earth and seas founded together upon nothing yet firm, and recalls the old conjecture of a first earth as a crust or shell over the waters until the deluge broke it in.

Clarke keeps the plain wonder — land separated from the waters, mountains raised above the flood, the earth established and unshaken for all the ocean's ragings; Wesley takes the seas for all the waters, sea, rivers, and the abyss in the bowels of the earth.

Ellicott sets the image among its kindred (Ps. 136:6; Prov. 8:25-29; Job 26:7, the earth hung on nothing) and traces the water-foundation idea to the phenomenon of springs; Keil and Delitzsch hear the procession arriving at the citadel gates, insisting the 'doors of eternity' be so rendered, not 'of the world' (against Luther).

Henry finds three grounds of God's title — he made the earth from nothing, made it as none else could (a foundation of seas bearing a world), and continues it so it abides through the generations (Eccl. 1:4) — the floods a warning how uncertain earthly things are.

outliers.note: Records the old cosmological conjecture that the first earth stood over the waters as a crust or shell, until the deluge broke it in and formed the sea.

schools.summary: Henry hears the meditation rise from earth to another world, the immortal soul unsatisfied and asking to ascend to the hill where God dwells, Zion typifying the church visible and invisible (cf. Ps. 15:1); Spurgeon calls it uphill work for the creature to reach the Creator, the true Israel marked by character not race, and presses 'who shall stand' as who can continue there.
Gill, allowing the reference to Moriah and Zion, takes the church to be mystically intended — named for its visibility through profession of faith and its immovableness, being built on Christ.

Clarke reads it of who is holy enough to wait in God's temple and minister in the holy place; Wesley takes the hill for Zion or Moriah, God's sanctuary, and 'stand' for the posture of ministers — who shall serve God with his acceptation.

debates.question: What is 'the hill of the LORD' one must ascend?

sides.position: the church and heaven itself — the soul's ascent to communion with God in grace and glory
the earthly sanctuary — the literal holiness required to minister and stand before the ark

themes: who shall stand in the holy place

schools.summary: Gill: clean hands are named first as more visible, but the pure heart is first in being — no man has it naturally, God creating and purifying it by faith, whence flow the clean hands that signify a holy conversation (washing of hands the token of innocence).

Clarke reads clean hands of an irreproachable conscience, the pure heart of one without deceit or unholy passion, and 'not lifted his soul unto vanity' of no idolatrous inclination; Wesley: the pure heart orders its very thoughts by God's word, and 'vanity' is the vain things of life — honours, riches, pleasures — which such a man does not value, making God his portion.

Ellicott brings the philology: the margin 'my soul' for 'his soul' (confirmed by the Alexandrian LXX; Rabbis take soul='name,' so to take the name in vain), 'vanity' as falsehood (Job 31:5), 'deceitfully' literally 'to fraud'; the LXX and Vulgate add 'to his neighbour' from Ps. 15.

Augustine reads toward eternity: the pure in thought 'hath not received his soul in vain,' not reckoning it among things that pass but, feeling it immortal, longing for an unchangeable eternity, and so, like things eternal, not swearing deceitfully.

outliers.note: Reports the marginal reading 'my soul' for 'his soul' (Alexandrian LXX), and the Rabbinic gloss soul='name,' so that 'lift up the soul to vanity' becomes 'take the name in vain.'

themes: clean hands and a pure heart
not lifted up his soul unto vanity
the pure heart first in being

schools.summary: Gill reads the future as present ('who receives') — the man fit to abide in the church has received every spiritual blessing in Christ, especially pardon, with adoption and a right to eternal life, the 'righteousness' being the substance of that blessing.

Henry unfolds a chain of privilege — blessed, justified and sanctified (the righteousness they hunger for, Matt. 5:6), and saved, for where God gives righteousness he designs salvation and brings the meet safely to heaven.

Clarke hears an allusion to Obed-edom, blessed while the ark lodged with him, and reads 'righteousness' as mercy crowning the fidelity it first created; Wesley keeps 'the blessing' broad — grace and glory and all good things.
Ellicott makes righteousness the real blessing from God: that virtue is her own reward is the moral statement, the highest religious statement being Christ's Beatitudes.

themes: righteousness from the God of his salvation

schools.summary: Gill takes the generation for the children of God, accounted by him for a generation, who seek him first and with their whole hearts, and seek him in Christ where alone he is found.

Henry hears a praying people, a remnant in every age accounted to the Lord for a generation (Ps. 22:30), joined both to God in prayer and to the people of God in the communion of saints — all who strive in prayer the spiritual seed of Jacob.

Clarke holds 'Elohey, O God' has dropped from most Hebrew MSS but survives in two of Kennicott's and the versions, so the line reads 'O God of Jacob,' with Selah a mark of confirmation; Wesley's margin likewise supplies 'O God of Jacob,' reading 'face' as God's grace and favour.
Ellicott agrees flatly that the address 'O Jacob' is certainly wrong, many critics rightly inserting 'O God of' after the LXX and Syriac.

debates.question: Does the last clause read 'O Jacob' or 'O God of Jacob'?

sides.position: emend to 'O God of Jacob' — the divine name dropped from the text, restored from the versions
retain the received 'O Jacob' — the patriarch (or his seed) the pattern of every seeker, though the marginal 'O God of Jacob' is acknowledged

schools.summary: Gill rejects the gates of hell (and the limbus) and even, strictly, the gates of heaven, following the Jewish interpreters — the gates of the temple, David prophesying their opening at Solomon's dedication when the ark should be carried in.

Clarke reads the shout of those preceding the ark, an allusion to a general's triumphal entry (with Callimachus's hymn to Apollo, 'Fall back, ye bolts'), the 'everlasting doors' a portcullis to be lifted; Wesley sees the temple doors, everlasting not for their materials but in opposition to the movable tabernacle.

Ellicott recovers the poetry — the LXX/Vulgate 'princes' for 'heads' and the 'portcullis' both blunt it; the old Jebusite gateways are too low for the approaching Monarch, and 'everlasting doors' is better 'ancient doors, gates of old,' the King of glory the returning glory that fled with Ichabod.

Henry, granting the first reference to the ark's entry, points the antiphon at Christ's ascension, the forerunner demanding entrance at the doors once shut against us (Gen. 3:24), angels asking 'Who is this King of glory?'; Spurgeon sees the representative Man rising from Olivet, the everlasting gates bidden give way before one higher than the heavens.

debates.question: Whose gates are the 'everlasting doors,' and whose entry is the King of glory's?

sides.position: the temple/citadel gates flung open for the ark's entry into Zion
the gates of heaven opened for the ascension of Christ

debates.question: How should 'everlasting doors' (pithei olam) and the personified 'gates' be rendered?

sides.position: 'everlasting doors' — personified gates lifting their heads (durable, of eternity, or as against the movable tabernacle)
'ancient doors, gates of old' — the venerable Jebusite gateways; 'princes' and 'portcullis' both wrong

outliers.note: Sets the antiphon beside two lines of Callimachus's hymn to Apollo ('Fall back, ye bolts; ye pond'rous doors, give way') as a heathen parallel to the demand for the gates to open.

themes: lift up your heads, O ye gates
the ascension of the King of glory

schools.summary: Gill hears the question put by the church, not in ignorance (the daughters of Jerusalem, the Pharisees) nor in scorn (Pharaoh), but wondering at the glories of Christ's person and desiring to know more of him.

Clarke reads a dialogue — those without demand, those within ask and answer 'Jehovah, come to his imperial city, conqueror and Saviour of Israel' — and presses a resurrection reading, the risen Christ claiming the glory won by his blood; Wesley keeps it plain: no ordinary person, no other than Jehovah, returned in triumph.

Ellicott feels the drama of the reluctant heathen gates that will not at once own the new-comer, whose title is the right of conquest ('Jehovah, the strong, the mighty, mighty in battle'); Keil and Delitzsch set out the answering verses of the antiphon as the psalm gives them.

outliers.note: Carries 'the LORD mighty in battle' beyond Israel's field to the resurrection — the risen Christ, having conquered sin, Satan, and death, claiming entrance into the glory he purchased by his blood.

themes: who is this King of glory
the challenge of the reluctant gates

schools.summary: Gill finds the reason for the repetition in the backwardness of churches and believers to open and let Christ in (Rev. 3:20), and to set forth his greatness and command awe; some take the two liftings-up for a twofold coming (second temple, then last judgment), but Gill prefers the certainty of his spiritual coming.

Wesley reads the repetition as spoken to awaken the dulness of mankind, so hardly brought to prepare for such solemnities, and to signify the matter's importance; Clarke marks that those within delay the first summons, so the demand must be raised again.

Henry observes that what is spoken once is spoken a second time, as usual in songs and with much beauty — entrance demanded again for the King who stands and knocks, to take possession as the rightful owner after the title has been contested.

themes: backwardness of the heart to open
the beauty of repetition in song

schools.summary: Gill reads the repeated question as asked to draw out a fuller account of the King's glorious Person than the first answer had told.

Ellicott hears a second challenge from the reluctant gates, inaugurating the great name by which the divine nature was especially known under the monarchy, 'the LORD of hosts' (origin and force at 1 Sam. 1:3).

Clarke marks the shifted form — 'who is this' before the ark appeared, 'who is He' now that the ark has arrived, 'here He is, to answer for himself,' whereupon the gates are thrown open and the procession admitted; Wesley unfolds 'of hosts' as command over all the armies of heaven and earth, angels, men, and every creature.

themes: who is this King of glory
the gates flung wide and the King brought home
